🚀 Looking for: AI/ML, Generative AI & Python Engineering Roles

Hi Hiring Managers and Recruiters,

I’m currently exploring my next opportunity in AI/ML, Generative AI, and Python engineering.

✨ One thing my resume probably doesn’t fully show is how much I care about making AI systems reliable after the model works.
I’ve worked on machine learning and GenAI systems where getting a prediction or response was only the beginning.
⚙️ A model can look strong in development and still struggle in production if the data changes.
🧠 A RAG system can produce a fluent answer and still be wrong if retrieval quality is poor.
🚨 An API can work perfectly in testing and still become a problem if latency, logging, monitoring, and error handling are treated as an afterthought.
Those experiences shaped how I approach AI engineering:
Build for reliability, not just demos.

For ML systems, that means validating data, monitoring model performance, and making failures easier to trace.

For RAG systems, that means grounding responses in retrieved context, checking relevance, using fallbacks when context is weak, and keeping source traceability.

For production services, that means clean Python code, modular APIs, logging, monitoring, versioning, and deployment workflows that make issues easier to detect and resolve.
And for AI in general, I’d rather build something dependable and explainable than something impressive only in a demo.

💡 The kind of work I enjoy most sits at the intersection of AI and software engineering — where models, APIs, data, infrastructure, and reliability all have to work together.
⚡ I enjoy taking AI beyond the prototype stage — turning ideas into systems that are usable, testable, observable, and production-ready.
I’m currently looking for opportunities in:
🔹 AI/ML Engineering
🔹 Generative AI
🔹 LLM/RAG Engineering
🔹 Applied AI
🔹 Python Engineering
🔹 MLOps
I’m open to contract, C2C, W-2, and full-time opportunities, including remote, hybrid, and relocation.
📄 Resume attached.

🤝 If you’re hiring in this space, know someone who is, or think my background could be a fit for your team, I’d be happy to connect.
🔁 Feel free to comment, message me, or share this post with someone in your network.

📍 Sometimes the right opportunity starts with a simple connection.

Entry-level hiring did not contract because of a downturn.

Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found that workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations now sit 19 percent below where they would be had they kept pace with their less-exposed peers. Experienced workers show no comparable gap. Same companies. Same roles.

The mechanism is hiring, not separations. Companies did not fire the junior cohort. They stopped opening the door.

For founders, that is not a labor market story. It is a role architecture problem. Every seat you open now requires someone who arrives already knowing, which moves your compensation floor, empties your bench, and turns every future leadership opening into an external search.

The full piece covers what the entry rung was actually doing for the business, and the three tests that separate a role that genuinely requires experience from one that just requires documentation.

Good news!  The hiring market is improving, but companies are not simply refilling the jobs they eliminated.

ManpowerGroup’s Q4 2026 survey found that 43% of employers plan to increase staffing. More importantly, 62% of those employers are hiring because the roles and skills they need are changing. Only 32% are focused on traditional backfills.

That is the real story.

I see this as a workforce reallocation, not a return to the old hiring market.

Companies need people who can help them implement AI, govern data, modernize platforms, strengthen cybersecurity, and turn technology investments into measurable business results.

The mistake is waiting until a project is underway to determine whether those skills exist internally. By then, the strongest specialized talent is often already committed elsewhere.

The companies that will move fastest are assessing skill gaps now and using the right combination of internal development, contract expertise, and permanent hiring to close them.

Hiring demand is returning. But it is returning with a different job description.
